label: thm:informal-2
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:informal-2}
The following are true:
\begin{itemize}
\item If one-way functions (respectively, infinitely-often one-way
functions) exist, then there exists an efficiently samplable
distribution family $D=\{D_n\}$ and a non-monotone compression
scheme $(\mathsf{Enc},\mathsf{Dec})$ with efficient encoding and decoding whose
expected encoding length on $D_n$ is exactly $H(D_n)$, but for
which every efficiently computable autoregressive model has
excess cross-entropy loss at least linear in the output length.
This lower bound holds for all sufficiently large lengths
(respectively, infinitely many lengths). 

        
                                                                            

                                                                                                                                                                                    
                                                                      
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                
   
\item If infinitely-often one-way functions do not exist, then, given a $\delta$-optimal compression scheme $(\mathsf{Enc},\mathsf{Dec})$ with efficient encoding and decoding for an efficiently samplable distribution family $D=\{D_n\}$, one can construct an efficiently computable autoregressive model which is statistically close to a $\delta$-optimal autoregressive model for $\mathcal{D}$.
\end{itemize}

title: Definition
body_md:
Given finite alphabets $\Sigma$ and $\Sigma'$, let $\mathsf{Enc} : \Sigma^* \rightarrow \Sigma'^*$ be a function defined with respect to some distribution $D$ with $\sup(D) \subseteq \Sigma^*$.

We refer to $\mathsf{Enc}$ as \textbf{prefix-free} if there do not exist elements $x \neq y$ and $i \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $x \in \Sigma^*$, $y \in \sup(D)$, and $\mathsf{Enc}(x) = (\mathsf{Enc}(y))_{< i}$ (i.e., $\mathsf{Enc}(x)$ is a prefix of $\mathsf{Enc}(y)$; we note, however, that this definition does allow an encoding of $y \in \sup(D)$ to be a prefix of an encoding of $x \not\in \sup(D)$).

                                                               
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    
                                                                          
                                                          

We refer to $\mathsf{Enc}$ as \textbf{monotone} if there exist efficiently computable orderings $\prec_\Sigma$ over $\Sigma$ and $\prec_{\Sigma'}$ over $\Sigma'$ such that, for any $x, y \in \Sigma^*$, $x \prec_{\Sigma^*} y$ if and only if $\mathsf{Enc}(x) \prec_{\Sigma'^*} \mathsf{Enc}(y)$, where $\prec_{\Sigma^*}$ is the lexicographic ordering\footnote{i.e., $x \prec_{\Sigma^*} y$ when there exists $i \in \mathbb{N}$ for which $x_{<i} = y_{<i}$ and either $\text{len}(y) > \text{len}(x) = i-1$ or $x_i \prec_{\Sigma} y_i$.} induced by $\prec_\Sigma$ on $\Sigma^*$ and respectively for $\prec_{\Sigma'^*}$. 

We consider any of the above properties to apply to a family of functions $\mathsf{Enc} = \lbrace \mathsf{Enc}_n \rbrace_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ as defined in Definition \ref{def:compression}, where $\mathsf{Enc}_n$ is defined with respect to a distribution $D_n$ for which $\sup(D_n) \subseteq \Sigma_n^{m(n)}$, if they apply to $\mathsf{Enc}_n$ and $D_n$ for each $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Furthermore, we say that such a family of functions has \textbf{efficient encoding} if there exists a polynomial $p(\cdot)$ such that $\mathsf{Enc}_n$ runs in time at most $p(n)$ for any $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and \textbf{efficient decoding} if there exists a polynomial $p'(\cdot)$ and a function family $\mathsf{Dec} = \lbrace \mathsf{Dec}_n \rbrace_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that, for each $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\mathsf{Dec}_n$ computes the inverse $\mathsf{Enc}_n^{-1}(c)$ of $\mathsf{Enc}_n$ for any codeword in its image (or returns $\bot$ if the input is not in the image) and additionally runs in time at most $p'(n)$.

name: Properties of compression

label: fact:decoding
title: Fact
body_md:
\label{fact:decoding}
Any monotone and efficiently encodable family of encodings $\mathsf{Enc} = \lbrace \mathsf{Enc}_n \rbrace_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is also efficiently decodable.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Consider a decoding algorithm that, given a codeword, performs binary search over the possible inputs in $\Sigma_n^{m(n)}$. This is possible due to monotonicity---it can be determined whether the correct decoding is lower or higher than a given input by comparing the respective codewords. Additionally, since there are $|\Sigma_n|^{m(n)}$ possible inputs in $\Sigma_n^{m(n)}$, binary search requires at most $O(m(n)\log |\Sigma_n|)$ iterations of $\mathsf{Enc}_n$. Since by definition $m(n)$ and $|\Sigma_n|$ are polynomial in $n$, and since $\mathsf{Enc}$ is itself efficient, this decoding process must likewise be efficient.

label: def:arithmetic_encoding
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:arithmetic_encoding}
Let $D$ be a discrete distribution and let $\prec$ be a total order over $\sup(D)$. Let $F : \sup(D) \rightarrow [0,1]$ by $F(x)=(\sum_{a\prec x}D(a))+1/2\cdot D(x)$. Then the \textbf{arithmetic encoding} $\mathsf{Enc} : \sup(D) \rightarrow \lbrace 0,1 \rbrace^*$ is defined such that, for $x \in \sup(D)$, $\mathsf{Enc}(x)$ is the first $(\ceil{-\log D(x)} +1)$ bits of $F(x)$.
head: environment
name: Arithmetic encoding

label: fact:arithmetic_encoding
title: Fact
body_md:
\label{fact:arithmetic_encoding}
For every distribution family $\mathcal{D} = \lbrace D_n \rbrace_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ and ordering $\prec$ over the corresponding input alphabet $\Sigma_n$, the functions $\mathsf{Enc}_n$ given by applying Definition \ref{def:arithmetic_encoding} to $D_n$ and $\prec$ (for any $n \in \mathbb{N}$) are one-to-one and monotone, and the scheme $\mathsf{Enc} = \lbrace \mathsf{Enc}_n \rbrace_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is prefix-free and compresses $\mathcal{D}$ to length $H(D_n) + 2$.
head: environment
name: Properties of arithmetic encoding, lemma 2.8

label: clm:arithmetic-properties
title: Claim
body_md:
\label{clm:arithmetic-properties}
For any alphabet $\lbrace \Sigma_n \rbrace_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$, any distribution family $\mathcal{D} = \lbrace D_n \rbrace_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ where $\sup(D_n) \subseteq \Sigma_n^{m(n)}$ and $-\log(D_n(x)) \leq \ell(n)$ for any $x \in \sup(D_n)$ and some polynomial $\ell(\cdot)$, and any ordering $\prec_n$ over $\Sigma_n$, if the cumulative distribution function $\sum_{a\preceq x}D_n(a)$ can be efficiently computed for any $x \in \Sigma^{m(n)}_n$, then there exists a prefix-free, monotone, and efficiently computable encoding $\mathsf{Enc} = \lbrace \mathsf{Enc}_n \rbrace_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ that additionally compresses $\mathcal{D}$ to length $H(D_n) + 2$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\mathsf{Enc}'_n$ be the arithmetic encoding given in Definition \ref{def:arithmetic_encoding}. Define $\mathsf{Enc}_n(x) = \mathsf{Enc}'_n(x)$ for all $x \in \sup(D_n)$; for $x \in \Sigma^{m(n)}_n \setminus \sup(D_n)$, let $\mathsf{Enc}_n(x)$ be the first $(\ell(n)+2)$ bits of the CDF $\sum_{a\prec x}D(a)$ (or $1^{\ell(n)+2}$ if the CDF is 1, i.e., $x \succ y$ for all $y \in \sup(D_n)$) with the binary representation of $x$ ordered by $\prec_n$ appended.

Prefix-freeness holds because, by Fact \ref{fact:arithmetic_encoding}, $\mathsf{Enc}_n$ is prefix-free when restricted to $\sup(D_n)$, and furthermore there cannot exist $x \in \Sigma^{m(n)}_n \setminus \sup(D_n)$ and $y \in \sup(D_n)$ where $\mathsf{Enc}_n(x)$ is a prefix of $\mathsf{Enc}_n(y)$ because, by definition, $\mathsf{Enc}_n(x)$ must be strictly longer than $\mathsf{Enc}_n(y)$.

To show monotonicity, consider some $x, y \in \Sigma^{m(n)}_n$ with $x \prec_n y$. If $x, y \in \sup(D_n)$, we conclude that $\mathsf{Enc}_n(x) < \mathsf{Enc}_n(y)$ by Fact \ref{fact:arithmetic_encoding}. If the first $(\ell(n)+2)$ bits of $\mathsf{Enc}_n(x)$ and $\mathsf{Enc}_n(y)$ are identical (which can only happen when $x, y \not\in \sup(D_n)$ and furthermore there is no $z \in D_n$ with $x \prec_n z \prec_n y$), we conclude that $\mathsf{Enc}_n(x) < \mathsf{Enc}_n(y)$ by the definition of $\mathsf{Enc}_n$ (since the following part of each of $\mathsf{Enc}_n(x)$ and $\mathsf{Enc}_n(y)$ is the binary representation of $x$ and $y$, respectively). Otherwise, it must be the case that $x$ and $y$ do not have the same CDF with respect to $D_n$, and so we conclude that $\mathsf{Enc}_n(x) < \mathsf{Enc}_n(y)$ because the respective prefixes of the encodings (which are prefixes of the respective CDFs) must be strictly ordered. 

To show that $\mathsf{Enc}_n$ can be efficiently computed: if $\sum_{a\preceq x}D_n(a)$ can be efficiently computed, then so can 
\[ D_n(x) = \sum_{a \preceq x}D_n(a) - \sum_{a\preceq x^-}D_n(a) \]
(where $x^-$ is the predecessor of $x$ under $\prec$) and consequently
\[ \sum_{a\prec x}D_n(a) = \sum_{a\preceq x}D_n(a) - D(x)\]
and thus $\mathsf{Enc}'_n(x)$ must be efficiently computable as well, which demonstrates efficient computability of $\mathsf{Enc}_n$ for $x \in \sup(D_n)$. For $x \not\in \sup(D_n)$, it suffices that the CDF $\sum_{a\prec x}D(a)$ is efficiently computable.

Finally, we remark that the encoding length of every $x \in \sup(D_n)$ is identical between $\mathsf{Enc}'_n$ and $\mathsf{Enc}_n$; therefore, the expected encoding length with respect to $D_n$ must remain unchanged.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: We note the assumption in the above claim that we have an effective \emph{a priori} bound of $p(n)+1$ on the length of the arithmetic encoding $\mathsf{Enc}'_n(x)$. Without such a bound, one can still prove a similar result by truncating the arithmetic encoding to a suitably large polynomial length $\ell(n)$ and appending the binary representation of $x$ to any truncated encoding, even for $x \in \sup(D_n)$ with non-zero $D_n(x)$. Since any $x \in \sup(D_n)$ must have $D_n(x) \leq 2^{-\ell(n)}$ for its encoding to be affected, and there are at most $|\Sigma_n|^{m(n)}$ possible codewords, as long as $\ell(n)$ is selected so that $2^{\ell(n)} \gg |\Sigma_n|^{m(n)}$, this will lose at most an exponentially small fraction of a bit in the output length. We, however, choose instead to assume an \emph{a priori} bound $\ell(n)$ since, in the setting we consider, any efficiently computable family of autoregressive models must produce a distribution family $\mathcal{D} = \lbrace D_n \rbrace_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ where the arithmetic encoding length is polynomially bounded anyway.

label: clm:optimal-encoding
title: Claim
body_md:
\label{clm:optimal-encoding}
Let $D, D'$ be distributions on $\Sigma^m$ and $\mathsf{Enc}$ be an encoding such that, for any element $x \in \sup(D')$:
\[ \text{len}(\mathsf{Enc}(x)) \leq \log(1/D'(x)) + \alpha \]
Then, for any distribution $D$ (with $\sup(D) \subseteq \sup(D')$):
\[ \mathbf{E}_{x \leftarrow D}[\text{len}(\mathsf{Enc}(x))]  \leq H(D) + KL(D \; || \; D') + \alpha \]

title: Definition
body_md:
The \textbf{cross-entropy} of a distribution $D_2$ relative to a distribution $D_1$ is given by:
\[ H(D_1, D_2) = - \mathbf{E}_{x \leftarrow D_1} [\log D_2(x)] = - \sum_{x \in \sup(D_1)} D_1(x) \log D_2(x) \]

label: fact:cross-kl
title: Fact

title: Proof
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: Given an alphabet $\Sigma$ and a maximum output length $m$,\footnote{We can assume without loss of generality that outputs of length less than $m$ are padded to length $m$ by a special $\mathsf{End}$ token.} we define an \textbf{autoregressive model} $\mathcal{M}$ over $\Sigma^m$ to be a collection of distributions $\lbrace \mathcal{M}_{t} \rbrace_{t \in \Sigma^{< m}}$ where every distribution $\mathcal{M}_t$ has support $\sup(\mathcal{M}_t) \subseteq \Sigma$. We define the induced distribution $D_\mathcal{M}$ to be the distribution of complete outputs resulting from the process of starting with an empty string $t$ and iteratively appending a sample from $\mathcal{M}_t$ to $t$ $m$ times to construct a length-$m$ string $t \in \Sigma^m$.
head: environment

label: clm:loss-kl
title: Claim
body_md:
\label{clm:loss-kl}
For alphabet $\Sigma$, maximum length $m$, and a fixed training distribution $D$ with support $\sup(D) \subseteq \Sigma^m$, if there exist an autoregressive model $\mathcal{M}$ over $\Sigma^m$ and constant $\delta$ such that $\mathcal{M}$ is $\delta$-optimal with respect to $D$,
then, for any autoregressive model $\mathcal{M}^*$ defined over $\Sigma^m$:
\[KL(D \; || \; D_\mathcal{M}) - KL(D \; || \; D_{\mathcal{M}^*}) \leq \delta \]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $m$ be the maximum output length of a sample from $D$. We can apply the chain rule and Fact \ref{fact:cross-kl} to show:
\begin{align*}
KL(D \; || \; D_\mathcal{M}) &\; = \sum_{i \in [m]} \mathbf{E}_{t_{<i} : t \leftarrow D} [KL(D_{t_{<i}} \; || \; \mathcal{M}_{t_{<i}})]  \\
&\; = \sum_{i \in [m]} \mathbf{E}_{t_{<i} : t \leftarrow D} [H(D_{t_{<i}}, \mathcal{M}_{t_{<i}}) - H(D_{t_{<i}})]  \\
\end{align*}
where $D_{t_{<i}}$ is defined analogously to $\mathcal{M}_{t_{<i}}$ (i.e., the next-token distribution given prefix $t_{<i}$) for the training distribution $D$. Furthermore:
\begin{align*}
&\;  \sum_{i \in [m]} \mathbf{E}_{t_{<i} : t \leftarrow D} [H(D_{t_{<i}}, \mathcal{M}_{t_{<i}})]  \\
= &\; - \sum_{i \in [m]} \mathbf{E}_{t_{<i} : t \leftarrow D} [\mathbf{E}_{t_{i} \leftarrow D_{t_{<i}}} [\log \mathcal{M}(t_i \; | \; t_{<i})]]  \\
= &\; - \sum_{i \in [m]} \mathbf{E}_{t_{\leq i} : t \leftarrow D} [\log \mathcal{M}(t_i \; | \; t_{<i})]  \\
= &\;  \mathbf{E}_{t \leftarrow D} \left[ - \sum_{i \in [m]} \log \mathcal{M}(t_i \; | \; t_{<i}) \right] =  \mathbf{E}_{t \leftarrow D} \left[ - \sum_{i \in [\text{len}(t)]} \log \mathcal{M}(t_i \; | \; t_{<i}) \right] = \mathbf{E}_{t \leftarrow D} [L(\mathcal{M}, t)] \\
\end{align*}
Importantly, since the training distribution $D$ is fixed, the entropy $H(D_{t_{<i}})$ is constant, as is its expectation over $t \leftarrow D$, which provides that $KL(D \; || \; D_\mathcal{M})$ and $\mathbf{E}_{t \leftarrow D} [L(\mathcal{M}, t)]$ are separated by the same additive constant for any model $\mathcal{M}$, implying the conclusion since we have 
\[ \mathbf{E}_{t \leftarrow D}[L(\mathcal{M}, t)] - \mathbf{E}_{t \leftarrow D}[L(\mathcal{M}^*, t)] \leq  \delta \]
by assumption of $\delta$-optimality.

label: clm:efficient-cumulative
title: Claim
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\emph{(1) $\rightarrow$ (2).} Consider the following procedure for computing $\Pr_{x \leftarrow D_{\mathcal{M}_n}}[x \preceq a]$:
\begin{itemize}
\item Let $p = 0$, $p' = 1$, and $i = 1$.
\item Let $M = (\mathcal{M}_n)_{a_{<i}}$, the next-token distribution for the $i^\text{th}$ token of $a$.
\item Set $p \leftarrow p + p' ( \sum_{t \in \text{sup}(M):t \prec a_i} M(t))$ and set $p' = p' \cdot M(a_i)$.
\item Repeat the previous two steps incrementing $i$ until $i = m(n)$ or $p' = 0$, then take $p \leftarrow p + p'$, terminate and return $p$.
\end{itemize}
Correctness holds because each iteration adds the probability that $x \leftarrow D_{\mathcal{M}_n}$ has $x_{<i} = a_{<i}$ but $x_i \prec a_i$ (and the final step $p \leftarrow p + p'$ adds the probability that $x = a$), and the sum of those probabilities is precisely $\Pr_{x \leftarrow D_{\mathcal{M}_n}}[x \preceq a]$.

Efficiency holds because, since $|\Sigma|$ is polynomial, we compute $M(t) = \mathcal{M}_n(t \; | \; a_{<i})$ at most a polynomial number of times in each iteration of the loop, which itself iterates a polynomial number $p(n)$ of times. 

\emph{(2) $\rightarrow$ (1).} 
                                                                                                                                                            
This follows since 

\[\mathcal{M}_n(t_i \; | \; t_{<i}) = \frac{\Pr_{x \leftarrow D_{\mathcal{M}_n}}[x_{\leq i} = t_{\leq i}]}{\Pr_{x \leftarrow D_{\mathcal{M}_n}}[x_{< i} = t_{< i}]} =  \frac{\Pr_{x \leftarrow D_{\mathcal{M}_n}}[x \preceq t_{\leq i}^\top] - \Pr_{x \leftarrow D_{\mathcal{M}_n}}[x \preceq t_{\leq i}^\bot]}{\Pr_{x \leftarrow D_{\mathcal{M}_n}}[x \preceq t_{<i}^\top] - \Pr_{x \leftarrow D_{\mathcal{M}_n}}[x \preceq t_{<i}^\bot]}\]
where $t_{<i}^\top$ is the $\prec$-greatest element of $\Sigma_n^{m(n)}$ with $t_{<i}$ as a prefix and $t_{<i}^\bot$ is the $\prec$-greatest element of $\Sigma_n^{m(n)}$ with a prefix $(t^\bot)_{<i} \prec t_{<i}$, and respectively for $t_{\leq i}^\top$ and $t_{\leq i}^\bot$.

body_md:
By Claim \ref{clm:loss-kl}, we have $KL(D \; || \; D_\mathcal{M}) \leq \delta$ (as the optimum is attained at $D = D_\mathcal{M}$ which results in a divergence of 0). By Claim \ref{clm:optimal-encoding}:
\[ \mathbf{E}_{x \leftarrow D}[\text{len}(\mathsf{Enc}(x))] \leq H(D) + KL(D \; || \; D_\mathcal{M}) + \alpha \leq H(D) + \delta + \alpha  \]

label: thm:compression-llm
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(For ease of notation, we omit the parameter $n$ and demonstrate the following for any $n \in \mathbb{N}$.)
We wish to define a model $\mathcal{M}^\mathsf{Enc}$ that induces a distribution $D_\mathcal{M}$ with a corresponding efficient random sampler $\mathsf{Sample} : \lbrace 0,1 \rbrace^{*} \to \Sigma^{m(n)}$ to be defined subsequently (that is, $D_\mathcal{M} = \lbrace c \leftarrow \lbrace 0,1 \rbrace^{*}: \mathsf{Sample}(c) \rbrace$). We will start by making the simplifying assumption that 
we know a bound $\ell(\cdot)$ such that $\text{len}(\mathsf{Enc}_{n}(x)) \leq \ell(n)$ for all $x \in \Sigma^{m(n)}$ (note that such a polynomial $\ell$ exists since $\mathsf{Enc}$ is efficient). $\mathsf{Sample}$, given a string $c \in \lbrace 0,1 \rbrace^{\ell(n)}$, does as follows:
\begin{itemize}
    \item Find the largest $x \in \Sigma^{m(n)}$ with $\mathsf{Enc}(x)\le c$. (findable by binary search over $\Sigma^{m(n)}$).\footnote{If no such $x$ exists, output the smallest element of $\Sigma^{m(n)}$.}
    \item Find the smallest $i$ such that $\mathsf{Dec}(c_{\leq i}) \neq \bot$ (where, leveraging monotonicity of $\mathsf{Enc}$, we define $\mathsf{Dec}$ per Fact \ref{fact:decoding}).
    \item If there is no such $i$, output $x$. Otherwise output $\mathsf{Dec}(c_{\leq i})$.
\end{itemize}
By Fact \ref{fact:decoding} and monotonicity of $\mathsf{Enc}$, $\mathsf{Dec}$ is efficiently computable, and thus $\mathsf{Sample}$ is as well. 
Furthermore, we make the following claim that $\mathsf{Sample}$ is \emph{weakly} monotone (which nonetheless is sufficient for our proof): 

\begin{claim*}
\label{clm:monotone-sampler}
     $\mathsf{Sample}$ is weakly monotone: for any $c_1, c_2 \in \lbrace 0,1 \rbrace^{\ell(n)}$, if $c_1 < c_2$, then $\mathsf{Sample}(c_1) \preceq \mathsf{Sample}(c_2)$.
\end{claim*}
\begin{proof}
    This follows from the fact that, since $\mathsf{Enc}$ is monotonic and $\mathsf{Dec}$ inverts $\mathsf{Enc}$ on its domain, $\mathsf{Dec}$ must also be monotonic. If both $c_1$ and $c_2$ have prefixes $(c_1)_{\leq i_1}$ and $(c_2)_{\leq i_2}$ with valid decodings, then $(c_1)_{\leq i_1} \leq(c_2)_{\leq i_2}$, and the same is true of the respective decodings by monotonicity. In the case where no prefix of $c_1$ has a valid decoding, $\mathsf{Sample}$ returns the last valid input whose encoding is smaller than $c_1$, which by monotonicity cannot be larger than $\mathsf{Dec}(c_2)$ (or, in the case that $c_2$ also has no prefix with a valid decoding, the last valid input whose encoding is smaller than $c_2$) without contradicting the assumption that $c_1 < c_2$. Finally, if no prefix of $c_2$ has a valid decoding but there is
such a prefix for $c_1$, then
$
\mathsf{Enc}(\mathsf{Sample}(c_1)) \le c_1 < c_2$.
Thus $\mathsf{Sample}(c_1)$ is a candidate in the search for the
largest $x$ satisfying $\mathsf{Enc}(x) \le c_2$. Since
$\mathsf{Sample}(c_2)$ returns that largest candidate, we obtain
$
\mathsf{Sample}(c_1) \preceq \mathsf{Sample}(c_2)$.

\end{proof}


We first need to argue that $KL( D \; || \; D_\mathcal{M}) \leq \delta$; towards that, we first observe that, for any $x \in \sup(D)$, $D_\mathcal{M}(x) \geq 2^{-\text{len}(\mathsf{Enc}(x))}$. This is true because, whenever $c$ is drawn such that it has $\mathsf{Enc}(x)$ as a prefix (which happens with precisely probability $2^{-\text{len}(\mathsf{Enc}(x))}$), that prefix is shorter than the maximum length $\ell(n)$ by assumption, and it is also the shortest correctly decodable prefix by prefix-freeness of $\mathsf{Enc}$, and thus $x$ will be sampled. From here, Fact \ref{fact:cross-kl} implies:
\[ KL( D \; || \; D_\mathcal{M}) = H(D, D_\mathcal{M}) - H(D) \]
But for any $x \in \sup(D)$, since $D_\mathcal{M}(x) \geq 2^{-\text{len}(\mathsf{Enc}(x))}$:
\[ -\log D_\mathcal{M}(x) \leq \text{len}(\mathsf{Enc}(x)) \]
and thus, by our original assumption about the compression loss of $\mathsf{Enc}$:
\[ - \mathbf{E}_{x \leftarrow D}[\log D_\mathcal{M}(x)] \leq \mathbf{E}_{x \leftarrow D}[\text{len}(\mathsf{Enc}(x))] \leq H(D) + \delta \]
But $- \mathbf{E}_{x \leftarrow D}[\log D_\mathcal{M}(x)]$ is exactly the cross-entropy $H(D, D_\mathcal{M})$, so:
\[ KL( D \; || \; D_\mathcal{M}) \leq (H(D) + \delta) - H(D) = \delta \]
as desired.

Thus far, we have given a description of the induced distribution $D_\mathcal{M}$ in terms of the random sampler $\mathsf{Sample}$, but not constructed the actual model $\mathcal{M}^\mathsf{Enc}$ nor shown that it is efficiently computable. Fortunately, Claim \ref{clm:efficient-cumulative} provides both of these as long as we can efficiently compute $\Pr_{x \leftarrow D_\mathcal{M}} [x \preceq y]$ for any $y \in \Sigma^{m(n)}$.\footnote{While Claim \ref{clm:efficient-cumulative} technically only provides efficient computability on prefixes with non-zero probability of occurrence, we note that we can trivially assign an arbitrary next-token distribution to prefixes with zero probability without changing $D_\mathcal{M}$.} However, we claim that, using the efficiency of $\mathsf{Sample}$ and Claim \ref{clm:monotone-sampler}, we can do precisely this:

\begin{claim*}
\label{clm:cdf}
    For any $y \in \Sigma^{m(n)}$, $\Pr_{x \leftarrow D_\mathcal{M}} [x \preceq y]$ can be efficiently computed.
\end{claim*}

\begin{proof}
    If we can efficiently determine the largest $c \in \lbrace 0,1 \rbrace^{\ell(n)}$ such that $\mathsf{Sample}(c) \leq y$ (taking $c = 0^{\ell(n)}$ if there is no such $c$), then we can immediately determine that (taking $c$ as an integer) $\Pr_{x \leftarrow D_\mathcal{M}} [x \preceq y] = (c+1)/2^{\ell(n)}$, as sampling from $D_\mathcal{M}$ is by definition equivalent to sampling $\mathsf{Sample}(c)$ for uniformly random $c \in \lbrace 0,1 \rbrace^{\ell(n)}$. And weak monotonicity from Claim \ref{clm:monotone-sampler} is sufficient to show that we can find such a $c$ using binary search over $\lbrace 0,1 \rbrace^{\ell(n)}$, which must run in time polynomial in $n$ since it requires at most $\ell(n)$ iterations (which we know is polynomial) and each iteration requires computing $\mathsf{Sample}$ and comparing elements of $\Sigma^{m(n)}$, both of which are efficient.
\end{proof}
Thus, by Claim \ref{clm:efficient-cumulative}, we have constructed an efficiently computable autoregressive model $\mathcal{M}$ with induced distribution $D_\mathcal{M}$ that, as we have argued, suffices to complete the argument given an a priori bound of $\ell$ on the length of $\mathsf{Enc}(x)$.

\paragraph{Removing $\ell$.} Next, we explain how to remove the assumption that $\ell$ is known. First, we modify $\mathsf{Sample}$ to, rather than sampling $c \leftarrow \lbrace 0,1 \rbrace^{\ell(n)}$, instead lazily sample $c \leftarrow \lbrace 0,1 \rbrace^*$: specifically, during the binary search, each time $\mathsf{Sample}$ compares $c$ to some output $\mathsf{Enc}(y)$ for $y \in \Sigma^m$, if the length of the sampled $c$ is shorter than $\text{len}(\mathsf{Enc}(y))$, $\mathsf{Sample}$ draws new uniformly random bits of $c$ up to length $|\mathsf{Enc}(y)|$. We argue that the output of $\mathsf{Sample}$ is identical. Letting $x$ be the largest $x \in \Sigma^{m}$ such that $\mathsf{Enc}(x) \le c$, we notice that number of bits of $c$ sampled by $\mathsf{Sample}$ is at least $|\mathsf{Enc}(x)|$ by construction. Moreover, if (the $\ell$-bit long)  $c$ has a prefix $c_{\le i}$ which is a valid codeword, then by monotonicity $c_{\le i}$ is a prefix of $\mathsf{Enc}(x)$ (otherwise, $\mathsf{Enc}(x) < c_{\leq i} \leq c$, contradicting $x$ being the largest $x \in \Sigma^{m}$ such that $\mathsf{Enc}(x) \le c$). Thus, in this case, $\mathsf{Sample}$ must return $\mathsf{Dec}(c_{\leq i})$ as before; if there is no such prefix, then $\mathsf{Sample}$ by construction finds and returns $x$, as desired.


Similarly, when computing the CDF in Claim \ref{clm:cdf}, finding the largest $c$ such that $\mathsf{Sample}(c)\le y$ is done by binary search where the length of the string $c$ determined by the number of random bits $\mathsf{Sample}$ reads during its execution on $c$. In the $i^\text{th}$ step of the binary search, we know the prefix $c_{<i}$, and we learn the $i^\text{th}$ bit by comparing the output of $\mathsf{Sample}(c_{<i}||10^*)$ to $y$ (if $y$ is smaller, the next bit is $0$, where if $y$ is larger or equal the next bit is $1$). We terminate the search when, on the current prefix of $c$, the execution of $\mathsf{Sample}$ halts on the prefix without drawing any additional random bits. After $|c|$ steps, we learn the entire string $c$, and can then compute the CDF $\Pr_{x \leftarrow D_\mathcal{M}} [x \preceq y]$ as before by setting $\ell=|c|$.

label: clm:monotone-sampler
title: Claim
body_md:
\label{clm:monotone-sampler}
     $\mathsf{Sample}$ is weakly monotone: for any $c_1, c_2 \in \lbrace 0,1 \rbrace^{\ell(n)}$, if $c_1 < c_2$, then $\mathsf{Sample}(c_1) \preceq \mathsf{Sample}(c_2)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
This follows from the fact that, since $\mathsf{Enc}$ is monotonic and $\mathsf{Dec}$ inverts $\mathsf{Enc}$ on its domain, $\mathsf{Dec}$ must also be monotonic. If both $c_1$ and $c_2$ have prefixes $(c_1)_{\leq i_1}$ and $(c_2)_{\leq i_2}$ with valid decodings, then $(c_1)_{\leq i_1} \leq(c_2)_{\leq i_2}$, and the same is true of the respective decodings by monotonicity. In the case where no prefix of $c_1$ has a valid decoding, $\mathsf{Sample}$ returns the last valid input whose encoding is smaller than $c_1$, which by monotonicity cannot be larger than $\mathsf{Dec}(c_2)$ (or, in the case that $c_2$ also has no prefix with a valid decoding, the last valid input whose encoding is smaller than $c_2$) without contradicting the assumption that $c_1 < c_2$. Finally, if no prefix of $c_2$ has a valid decoding but there is
such a prefix for $c_1$, then
$
\mathsf{Enc}(\mathsf{Sample}(c_1)) \le c_1 < c_2$.
Thus $\mathsf{Sample}(c_1)$ is a candidate in the search for the
largest $x$ satisfying $\mathsf{Enc}(x) \le c_2$. Since
$\mathsf{Sample}(c_2)$ returns that largest candidate, we obtain
$
\mathsf{Sample}(c_1) \preceq \mathsf{Sample}(c_2)$.
head: environment

label: clm:cdf
title: Claim
body_md:
\label{clm:cdf}
    For any $y \in \Sigma^{m(n)}$, $\Pr_{x \leftarrow D_\mathcal{M}} [x \preceq y]$ can be efficiently computed.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: If we can efficiently determine the largest $c \in \lbrace 0,1 \rbrace^{\ell(n)}$ such that $\mathsf{Sample}(c) \leq y$ (taking $c = 0^{\ell(n)}$ if there is no such $c$), then we can immediately determine that (taking $c$ as an integer) $\Pr_{x \leftarrow D_\mathcal{M}} [x \preceq y] = (c+1)/2^{\ell(n)}$, as sampling from $D_\mathcal{M}$ is by definition equivalent to sampling $\mathsf{Sample}(c)$ for uniformly random $c \in \lbrace 0,1 \rbrace^{\ell(n)}$. And weak monotonicity from Claim \ref{clm:monotone-sampler} is sufficient to show that we can find such a $c$ using binary search over $\lbrace 0,1 \rbrace^{\ell(n)}$, which must run in time polynomial in $n$ since it requires at most $\ell(n)$ iterations (which we know is polynomial) and each iteration requires computing $\mathsf{Sample}$ and comparing elements of $\Sigma^{m(n)}$, both of which are efficient.

label: cor:compression-llm
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:compression-llm}
Given a polynomial-sized alphabet family $\Sigma = \lbrace \Sigma_n \rbrace_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ and polynomial maximum length $m(\cdot)$, there exists an oracle-aided sampling algorithm $\mathsf{Sample}^{(\cdot)}$ such that, for any family of distributions $\mathcal{D} = \lbrace D_n \rbrace_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$, function $\delta(\cdot)$, and prefix-free, monotone, and efficiently encodable family of encodings $\mathsf{Enc} = \lbrace \mathsf{Enc}_n \rbrace_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ where, for any $n \in \mathbb{N}$,
\[ \mathbf{E}_{x \leftarrow D_n} [\text{len}(\mathsf{Enc}_{n}(x))] \leq H(D_n) + \delta(n) \]
$\mathsf{Sample}^{(\cdot)}$ defines an efficiently computable family of randomized algorithms $\lbrace \mathsf{Sample}_n \rbrace_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that there exists a family of distributions $\lbrace D^*_n \rbrace_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ where, for any $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\mathsf{Sample}_n$ samples from $D^*_n$ and $KL(D_n \; || \; D^*_n) \leq \delta(n)$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
A family of functions $\mathcal{F} = \lbrace f_n \rbrace_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$, where $f_n : \lbrace 0,1 \rbrace^n \rightarrow \lbrace 0,1 \rbrace^n$, is \textbf{one-way} if $\mathcal{F}$ is efficiently computable but, for any non-uniform polynomial-time inverter $\mathcal{A}$, there is a negligible function $\epsilon(\cdot)$ such that for any $n \in \mathbb{N}$:
\[ \text{Pr} \left[x \leftarrow \lbrace 0,1 \rbrace^n : f(\mathcal{A}(1^n, f(x))) = f(x) \right] \leq \epsilon(n) \]

If the above instead holds for only \emph{infinitely many} $n \in \mathbb{N}$ for any non-uniform polynomial-time inverter $\mathcal{A}$, we say that $\mathcal{F}$ is \textbf{infinitely-often one-way}.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
For some output length $\ell(n) > n$, a family of efficiently computable functions $\mathcal{G} = \lbrace g_n \rbrace_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is referred to as a family of \emph{pseudorandom generators} (PRGs) if, for any polynomial-time distinguisher $D$ with output in $\lbrace 0,1 \rbrace$, there exists a negligible function $\epsilon(\cdot)$ such that for any $n \in \mathbb{N}$:
\[ \left| \text{Pr} \left[x \leftarrow U_n : D(1^n, g_n(x)) = 1 \right] - \text{Pr} \left[y \leftarrow U_{\ell(n)} : D(1^n, y) = 1 \right] \right| \leq \epsilon(n) \]
where $U_k$ represents the uniform distribution over $\lbrace 0,1 \rbrace^k$.
head: environment

label: thm:owf-separation
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:owf-separation}
Assuming the existence of one-way functions (respectively, infinitely-often one-way functions), there exists a family of efficiently samplable distributions $\mathcal{D} = \lbrace D_n \rbrace_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ and a prefix-free family of encodings $\mathsf{Enc} = \lbrace \mathsf{Enc}_n \rbrace_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ with efficient encoding and decoding such that $\mathbf{E}_{x \leftarrow D_n} [\text{len}(\mathsf{Enc}_{n}(x))] = H(D_n)$ for any $n \in \mathbb{N}$, but, given any efficiently computable family of autoregressive models $\lbrace \mathcal{M}_n \rbrace_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$, for any constant $\epsilon > 0$ and all sufficiently large (resp., infinitely many) $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the respective output distribution $D_{\mathcal{M}_n}$ is such that $KL(D_n \; || \; D_{\mathcal{M}_n}) \geq (1 - \epsilon)n$.\footnote{This implies that, for any constant $\delta$, $\mathcal{M}$ cannot be $\delta$-optimal with respect to $\mathcal{D}$.}
head: environment

title: Proof
head: environment

title: Claim
body_md: $\text{Pr} \left[y \leftarrow U_{2n} : \mathcal{A}(y) = 1 \right] \leq 2^{-c}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: $\mathbf{E}_{y \leftarrow U_{2n}}[D_{\mathcal{M}_n}(y, *)] = 2^{-2n}$, so this follows from Markov's inequality.
head: environment

title: Claim
body_md: For any constant $\epsilon' > 0$, $\text{Pr} \left[x \leftarrow U_{n} : \mathcal{A}(g_n(x)) = 1 \right] > \epsilon/2 - \epsilon'$ for all sufficiently large $n \in \mathbb{N}$ where $KL(D_n \; || \; D_{\mathcal{M}_n}) < (1 - \epsilon)n$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
This follows from the assumption that $KL(D_n \; || \; D_{\mathcal{M}_n}) < (1 - \epsilon)n$, and thus, by data processing, that $KL((D_n)_{\leq 2n} \; || \; (D_{\mathcal{M}_n})_{\leq 2n}) < (1 - \epsilon)n$ (where $(D_n)_{\leq 2n}$ represents the distribution of the first $2n$ bits of $D_n$, and respectively for $D_{\mathcal{M}_n}$). Thus:
\[ KL((D_n)_{\leq 2n} \; || \; (D_{\mathcal{M}_n})_{\leq 2n}) = \mathbf{E}_{y \leftarrow D_n}[\log(1/D_{\mathcal{M}_n}(y, *))] - H((D_n)_{\leq 2n}) < (1 - \epsilon)n \]
and so
\[ \mathbf{E}_{x \leftarrow U_n}[\log(1/D_{\mathcal{M}_n}(g_n(x), *))] = \mathbf{E}_{y \leftarrow D_n}[\log(1/D_{\mathcal{M}_n}(y, *))] < (1 - \epsilon)n + H((D_n)_{\leq 2n}) \leq (2-\epsilon)n \]
since $H((D_n)_{\leq 2n}) \le H(D_n) = n$. Now, by construction of $\mathcal{A}$, $\mathcal{A}$ outputs $1$ whenever $\log(1/D_{\mathcal{M}_n}(y, *)) < 2n-c$; by Markov's inequality and the above bound on the expectation, the probability that this is \emph{not} true (i.e., that $\mathcal{A}$ outputs $0$) when $y$ is given by $g_n(x)$ for $x \leftarrow U_n$ can be at most $\frac{(2-\epsilon)n}{2n-c}$, so the probability that $\mathcal{A}$ outputs $1$, then, must be at least 
\[ 1 - \frac{(2-\epsilon)n}{2n-c} = \frac{\epsilon n - c}{2n - c}\]
which asymptotically approaches $\epsilon/2$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$, implying the conclusion.

label: def:next-bit-predictor
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:next-bit-predictor}                                                                                                                                                                                                                     
  For alphabet $\Sigma$ and distribution $D$ over $\Sigma^{m}$, we say that an autoregressive model $\mathcal{M}$ is \textbf{$\epsilon$-approximately $\delta$-optimal} with respect to $D$ if there exists a model $\mathcal{M}'$ that is $\delta$-optimal with respect to $D$ and, $\Delta(\mathcal{D}_\mathcal{M},\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{M}'})\le \epsilon$.
head: environment

label: thm:owf-inverter-to-predictor
title: Theorem
body_md: \label{thm:owf-inverter-to-predictor} Let $\mathcal{D} = \lbrace D_n \rbrace_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a family of efficiently samplable distributions where each $D_n$ distributed over $\lbrace 0,1 \rbrace^{m(n)}$ for some polynomial $m(n)$. Then, for any function $\epsilon(n) \in 1/\mathsf{poly}(n)$, there exists a function $f$ such that, if $f$ is not an infinitely-often one-way function, then there exists an $\epsilon(n)$-approximate ($0$-optimal) efficiently computable autoregressive model for $\mathcal{D}$.
head: environment
name: Infinitely-often one-way functions and next-bit predictors

title: Proof
body_md:
\cite{il89} showed that for every family of efficiently samplable distributions $\mathcal{D}$ and for any $\epsilon'(n) \in 1/\mathsf{poly}(n)$, there exists a function $f$ such that, if $f$ is not an infinitely-often one-way function, then there exists a (non-uniform) efficient \emph{randomized} next bit-predictor $\mathsf{Pred}$ with \[\Pr_{t\leftarrow D_{n}}[\mathsf{Pred}(t_i \; | \; t_{<i})  \in D_n(t_i \; | \; t_{<i})(1-\epsilon', 1+\epsilon')]\ge 1-\epsilon'\]
for every sufficiently large $n \in \mathbb{N}$. We first notice that $\mathsf{Pred}$ can be made deterministic by fixing the randomness to the best possible string for each index $i$ as part of the non-uniform advice.

Next, we notice that $\mathsf{Pred}$ is already an $\epsilon=O(\epsilon'\cdot m(n))$-approximate model for $\mathcal{D}$, as the above promise on $\mathsf{Pred}$ implies that its output is close in statistical distance to the distribution $D_n$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: In fact, Theorem \ref{thm:owf-inverter-to-predictor} can be made stronger: one can show the existence of such a model based on an inverter to a \emph{specific} function (as opposed to complete non-existence of infinitely-often one-way functions, which would imply the existence of an inverter for \emph{every} function). In particular, \cite{il89} showed that for any $\epsilon(n) \in 1/\mathsf{poly}(n)$, there exists a pair of efficient oracle-aided algorithms $(f^{(\cdot)},\mathsf{Pred}^{(\cdot)})$ such that, given a sampler $\mathsf{Sample}$ for an ensemble of samplable distributions $\mathcal{D}$, if there exists a polynomial-time algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ that, for all sufficiently large $n \in \mathbb{N}$, inverts $f^{\mathsf{Sample}}$ with probability $1/2$, then $\mathsf{Pred}^A$ is an $\epsilon$-approximate next-bit predictor for $\mathcal{D}$. (In particular, $f^{\mathsf{Sample}}(x_1,\dots,x_t)= g^{\mathsf{Sample}}(x_1),\dots,g^{\mathsf{Sample}}(x_t)$, where $g^{\mathsf{Sample}}(r,h,i,j)=(i,j,h,\mathsf{Sample}(r)_{\le i}, h(r)_{\le j})$, $h$ is a 2-universal hash function, and $t \in O(n/\epsilon)$.)
head: environment

label: thm:owf-inverter-to-predictor-2
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first notice that, for any $n$ we can construct a distribution $\mathcal{D}'_n$ such that $KL(D_n,D'_n)\le \delta(n)$.
Specifically, we showed in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:compression-llm} that the distribution $D_\mathcal{M}$, which can be thought of as sampling a uniformly random string and decoding the (unique) codeword that is a prefix of that string, is not only efficiently samplable even when $\mathsf{Enc}$ is non-monotone (it requires only that $\mathsf{Enc}$ has an efficient decoding algorithm $\mathsf{Dec}$), but induces a model $\mathcal{M}^*$ which is $\delta$-optimal with respect to $\mathcal{D}$. (We note that $\mathsf{Sample}$ as written requires binary search and thus monotonicity to be efficient, but, if weak monotonicity is not needed, one can replace this step while preserving $\delta$-optimality by returning an arbitrary output if the given random string has no validly decodable prefix.)

Next, while $\mathcal{M}^*$ is not necessarily efficiently computable if $\mathsf{Enc}$ (and thus $\mathsf{Sample}$) is non-monotone, Theorem \ref{thm:owf-inverter-to-predictor} shows directly that, if infinitely-often one-way functions do not exist, then for any function $\epsilon(n) \in 1/\mathsf{poly}(n)$ there is a model $\mathcal{M}$ that is $\epsilon(n)$-approximate with respect to $D_\mathcal{M}$ and thus an $\epsilon(n)$-approximate $\delta$-optimal model for $\mathcal{D}$.

label: def:pseudoentropy
title: Definition
head: environment

label: cor:pseudoentropy
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:pseudoentropy}
Given polynomial maximum length $m(\cdot)$ and family of distributions $\mathcal{D} = \lbrace D_n \rbrace_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ where $D_n$ is a distribution over $\lbrace 0,1 \rbrace^{m(n)}$, for some function $\delta(\cdot)$, $\mathcal{D}$ has next-bit pseudoentropy at least $H(D_n) + \delta(n)$ if and only if, for any polynomial $p(\cdot)$, for every efficiently computable autoregressive model family $\mathcal{M} = \lbrace M_n \rbrace_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ and every sufficiently large $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $M_n$ is not  $(\delta(n)-1/p(n))$-optimal with respect to $D_n$.
head: environment

label: cor:incompressibility-pseudoentropy
title: Corollary
head: environment

label: cor:pseudoentropy-incompressibility
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:pseudoentropy-incompressibility}
Given polynomial maximum length $m(\cdot)$ and family of distributions $\mathcal{D} = \lbrace D_n \rbrace_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ where $D_n$ is a distribution over $\lbrace 0,1 \rbrace^{m(n)}$, if, for some function $k(\cdot)$, $\mathcal{D}$ has next-bit pseudoentropy at least $k(n)$, then, for any polynomial $p(\cdot)$, $\mathcal{D}$ cannot be monotonically compressed to length $k(n) - 1/p(n)$.
